title: Zhong Tou Yushu but missed the follow-on: patient capital also gets stuck by fund cycles
dek: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but in the 2023 round it couldn't follow on because its own USD fund was expiring and it was raising a new fund. Doubling down tests not just vision, but the match between fund and project timing.
why: A person who has done hard-tech VC for 17 years inside Singapore's sovereign capital system lays out the betting logic for chips, robotics and low-altitude economy, and candidly reviews why he missed ByteDance and the follow-on in Unitree.
who: Suitable for founders and investors focused on hard tech, robotics and the full cycle of USD fund raising, investing, managing and exiting, especially those who want to know how a sovereign-capital-backed VC makes independent judgments and reviews missed follow-ons.
skip: From 27:35 to 33:28, it covers Singapore clan associations, the Zhongyuan Festival and Chinese cohesion, which has little to do with investment judgment.

points.h: They started investing when chips were cheaper than potato chips
points.body: Vertex invested in semiconductors as early as 2011, and in 2012 in a new materials company making solid-state batteries. At the time, domestic VCs barely looked at these, because the internet was at its peak. Zheng Juncong told a joke: chips are called chips, and everyone thought a chip was cheaper than a potato chip, so nobody invested, because chips were imported and sold for only one US dollar each. He judged that chip technology content is extremely high, from millions of lines of code to billions of lines of code, and all electronic products, from cars to the cloud, need them. The pitch for investing in chips also changed with the times: first it was domestic production being tax-free, then iterating around the mobile phone supply chain, and now it's about being bottlenecked plus next-generation applications like optical computing.

points.h: IC can pass by half, and there's a golden share
points.body: Vertex's investment committee does not need a unanimous vote; a majority suffices, and they even hold ad hoc meetings on weekends if a project needs to go to IC. More unusual is the golden share: a partner has one chance a year to force investment in a company even if the IC did not approve it. Voting is secret; you don't know whether a partner voted for or against, because they don't want everyone doing favors for each other and abandoning independent judgment. The vote choice is also tied to project outcomes long-term: if a project fails but you voted for it, it will be traced back and counted in your score, and when distributing carry they will pull it out to look at. This mechanism is designed to force independent judgment, not personal favors.

points.h: They don't chase trends, because founders of fought-over projects get arrogant
points.body: Vertex explicitly does not invest in projects that are particularly sought after in the market. Zheng Juncong gave two reasons: first, everyone fighting drives up the valuation; second, when a founder is fought over, they focus on valuation, feel that investors are all flattering them, and won't do the company solidly, so the success rate is actually lower. They value founders who do technology solidly, have patience, want to create value, and don't rely on publicity. They have zero tolerance for financial fraud, because Singapore cares a lot about integrity and authenticity, and once fraud is discovered they will definitely withdraw. This style also explains why they haven't invested in many money-burning internet companies.

points.h: If choosing again on large models, still not investing, because it's like the internet
points.body: Over the past four years, the undisputed hot spot for investment in China has been AI large models, and Vertex didn't make a move in the first three or four years, which is very unusual among first-tier funds. Zheng Juncong's reasoning: large model startups in China have no advantage; the advantage will come from customers, data and application scenarios, and it needs to be big enough and able to burn a lot of money; it's essentially like the internet playbook, and the business model is still unclear. The two biggest internal voices were "this will definitely take off, China will definitely have large models" and "the model risk is high, it may continue to burn money like the internet, and existing large internet companies have a higher probability of success." He admits this discourages young investors who want to participate, but they held back from investing because they firmly believe hard tech is the advantage.

points.h: Singapore certification: swap chips and software, then export
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Singapore can help Chinese entrepreneurs solve two things: product internationalization and product security. Products made with China's manufacturing, design and innovation capabilities are wanted worldwide, but when they encounter geopolitics, politicians will obstruct them on the grounds that "Chinese products are unsafe, robots might carry things and hit people on the street." Singapore, as a neutral, transparent and reputable country, can achieve "Citified by Singapore"—chips certified here, or swapped for chips here, software here, and then exported from here, allowing products to enter other countries. He also criticized "Singapore Washing": companies that move here just to slap on a label, without actual operations and R&D, is the term he least wants to hear.

points.h: Boston Dynamics costs over a hundred thousand USD, Wang Xingxing sells for over ten thousand
points.body: In 2019, Zheng Juncong went to Boston for a board meeting and visited Boston Dynamics. He wanted to buy a robot dog, but they said it wasn't for sale, and the cost was about a hundred thousand USD. After returning to China, he judged that China is strong in hardware and someone must be doing it, so he had his team search all Chinese robotics teams and found Wang Xingxing. At the time, the robot dog was already very agile, could stand up and bow. He asked if it was controlled by AI, and Wang Xingxing said no, it used his own algorithm. When asked about cost, Wang Xingxing didn't mention cost, only said it currently sells for about ten thousand USD. The same dog, others' cost is over a hundred thousand, he sells for over ten thousand; Zheng Juncong judged there was commercialization potential, and cost is a very important element in technological innovation.

points.h: Missed the follow-on in Unitree: fund expired, not enough bullets
points.body: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but the follow-on investment only came in September 2024, by which time Unitree had already made the G1 bipedal robot and its valuation had soared. Why didn't they follow on earlier? Zheng Juncong reviewed: when they invested, they saw a market of several billion, but didn't see that bipedal robots could be made; in the 2023 round, Matrix Partners and Shunwei came in, and they also wanted to invest, but their USD fund was just at the end of its term and they were raising a new fund, so they didn't have enough bullets to add to the position, and thus missed that round. He called it a huge regret, and said this incident made them reflect, and now the new fund requires starting to raise new capital once 65% is invested, reserving 20% to 30% for follow-on investments.

points.h: Wang Xingxing raised funds slowly, but that honed mass production consistency
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Wang Xingxing doesn't need to be better at fundraising; the current fundraising pace is actually the best. If back then he was very good at fundraising and raised a lot of money in the next round, the playbook might have been different, he would be flashy, burn more money, lack discipline in running the company, not nitpick cost details, and the models produced might not be profitable. After AI came, many companies want to copy Unitree, thinking the barrier isn't high, it's just algorithms, and they can catch up quickly with AI. Zheng Juncong says everyone can get algorithms to about the same level, but the real gap is mass production and consistency, which is built up from all past investment and time, and no second company in the market has his mass production consistency.

points.h: A crude way to judge bubbles: look at who is starting companies
points.body: When asked whether China's embodied intelligence has a bubble, Zheng Juncong said no, because the market is still expanding and in its creation phase. He gave a rough indicator for judging bubbles: when the entrepreneurs you attract are not real entrepreneurs, but people who were in big companies without entrepreneurial spirit, who see others succeed and raise money and jump out saying they also want to start a company, that's the node where a bubble appears. Now he sees entrepreneurs who are "I've done this and that," very strong, capable people. He quoted Lee Kuan Yew saying the market needs bubbles, like beer without foam isn't tasty, but too much foam isn't good either, it should be controlled at an appropriate proportion.

terms.def: Vertex's investment committee mechanism: a partner can, once a year, force investment in a project rejected by the IC.
Distributions to Paid-In Capital: the money LPs actually get back divided by the principal invested, the hardest metric sovereign funds use to assess GPs.
Refers to Chinese companies that only move their headquarters to Singapore for labeling, without actual operations and R&D.
Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, the core category of the low-altitude economy, using multiple electric rotors instead of a helicopter's single engine.
Using AI to research new materials, chemical structures and other problems humans cannot calculate.
